title: Emissions are not concentrations
subtitle: Trace a pollutant from its source to the air we measure.
paragraphs: An emissions inventory describes material released from sources over a defined area and period. An ambient concentration describes how much of a substance is present in a specified volume of air. These quantities answer different questions: one concerns release, while the other concerns the state of the atmosphere.

Concentrations reflect several interacting processes. Emissions add material, transport moves it between locations, chemical reactions transform it, and removal processes take it out of the atmosphere. A lower concentration at one location therefore cannot, by itself, establish that local emissions have fallen.

An air-quality model represents these processes together within a defined domain. Interpreting a scenario requires checking the emissions inputs, meteorological conditions, boundary conditions, and chemical representation. The modeled concentration is a result of that combined system, rather than a direct copy of the emissions inventory.

An organised estimate of releases by source, location and time.
Information supplied at the edges of a model domain.

title: When a surface is both a source and a sink
subtitle: Read the direction of ammonia exchange carefully.

sourceEvidence.needle: Exchange of pollutants between the atmosphere

paragraphs: The exchange of a pollutant between the atmosphere and a surface need not occur in only one direction. In a bidirectional representation, the direction depends on the relative concentrations associated with the air and the surface. The same land surface may consequently act as a source under one set of conditions and as a sink under another.

For ammonia, the surface representation includes compensation concentrations associated with soil and vegetation. When the atmospheric concentration exceeds the relevant surface concentration, deposition can occur. When it is lower, emission can occur. Resistance terms and environmental conditions affect the rate of exchange.

A reported net flux must therefore be interpreted using its sign convention and model configuration. A small net flux does not establish that both directional processes are absent. Likewise, treating every modeled surface flux as an emission would confuse atmospheric input with atmospheric removal.

terms.definition: Transfer that may occur from air to surface or from surface to air.
A surface-related concentration used to determine net exchange.
The signed result of opposing transfer contributions.

choices.explanation: Deposition is not conditional on all emissions being zero.

title: A good total can hide the wrong processes
subtitle: Look beneath a small net concentration change.
paragraphs: A model can reproduce a small net concentration change even when substantial production and removal occur during the same period. The net result combines contributions from emissions, transport, chemistry and other processes. Opposing contributions may cancel, leaving little apparent change in the reported concentration.

This cancellation can also conceal errors. An incorrect emissions contribution may be partly offset by an error of the opposite sign in another process. Agreement in the final concentration is useful evidence, but it does not prove that each process is represented correctly.

Process analysis diagnoses individual contributions. Integrated Process Rate analysis separates physical and overall chemical contributions, while Integrated Reaction Rate analysis examines selected reaction rates and combinations. These diagnostics support an explanation of the result that cannot be obtained from a single total alone.

terms.definition: The result after increases and decreases have been combined.
Errors whose opposing effects partly cancel.
A diagnostic separation of process contributions.

title: Source contribution is not a control response
subtitle: Understand what an attribution result can tell you.
paragraphs: A source-apportionment analysis asks how selected sources contribute to modeled concentrations or deposition. A control experiment asks how those outputs change when an emission source is reduced or removed. The questions are related, but they are not identical.

One possible experiment runs the model with the usual emissions and then repeats it after removing a source. Interpreting the difference as that source’s contribution can be problematic in a nonlinear chemical system. Removing a large source changes the mixture in which other reactions occur, so the remaining sources may not behave as they did in the baseline.

A tagged source-apportionment method instead follows specified source information within a simulation, subject to the method’s species coverage and assumptions. Its results should be reported as attribution estimates. They should not automatically be read as the effect of an equally sized future emission reduction.

terms.definition: Allocation of modeled pollutant contributions to selected sources.
A reference simulation against which another case is compared.
A response that is not a fixed proportion of an input change.

title: Designing a sensitivity experiment
subtitle: Ask which input change the model is responding to.
paragraphs: Sensitivity describes the response of a model output to a specified change in an input or parameter. For an emissions experiment, one run may use the standard inputs and another an adjusted emission rate. The output difference must be interpreted in relation to the size and definition of the adjustment.

The cost of this direct comparison grows as more separate parameters are investigated. Direct sensitivity methods can propagate sensitivities within the model, providing another way to examine multiple parameters. Their applicability still depends on the model version, available scientific options and the outputs of interest.

A sensitivity result identifies a response under a defined setup. It does not automatically describe how probable the input change is, and it is not by itself a full uncertainty distribution. A clear report names the parameter, baseline, perturbation and output being compared.

terms.definition: A specified change made to an input or parameter.
The output response to a defined input change.
A probability-based description of uncertain values.

title: Compare like with like
subtitle: Time stamps and averaging periods can change a model evaluation.
paragraphs: Model evaluation requires pairing outputs with observations that describe comparable quantities. Matching a monitoring location to a model grid is only part of the task. The observation and simulation must also agree in species definition, units and the period represented by each value.

An hourly mean is not the same quantity as an instantaneous measurement or an hourly total. Time stamps may mark the beginning of an interval, and observations may be reported in a station’s local standard time. Ignoring these conventions can shift the comparison or combine incompatible quantities.

Daily or weekly comparisons also need the appropriate aggregation of the model data. A convenient file name or matching calendar date does not establish a correct pairing. Evaluation should document the averaging period, time-zone convention and spatial selection used to produce each matched pair.

title: Follow the mass through the model
subtitle: Connect a conservation principle with process equations.
paragraphs: A chemical transport model represents changes in atmospheric species using a conservation-based framework. Its equation includes contributions from transport, emissions, chemical reactions and removal. The computational grid defines the volumes over which these contributions are evaluated.

A species can be transformed into other species even when an underlying element is conserved. Consequently, conserving total elemental mass does not imply that every individual chemical species remains constant. Likewise, a concentration in one grid cell can change because material crosses its boundaries.

The numerical representation must maintain consistency between the grid, input fields and process calculations. Different horizontal projections or incompatible grid spacing across components would undermine the intended physical comparison. A scientifically useful interpretation connects the numerical setup to the conservation relationships it is meant to represent.

terms.definition: Accounting for material through changes, transport and sources or sinks.
A substance or modeled group represented by the chemistry.
The spatial cells used to carry out numerical calculations.

title: Why a precise estimate can still be wrong
subtitle: Separate random scatter from systematic error.
paragraphs: An estimate can be highly repeatable and still systematically miss the quantity of interest. Precision concerns agreement among repeated measurements, whereas accuracy concerns systematic departure from the true value. These properties should therefore be assessed separately.

Taking more independent observations can reduce random uncertainty in an estimated mean. It does not necessarily remove a bias caused by an unrepresentative sample or a flawed measurement method. Nor does it eliminate the real variation of a system across sites, times or operating conditions.

A defensible inventory first identifies and corrects known biases as far as possible, then quantifies remaining uncertainty under stated assumptions. Potential sources that cannot yet be quantified should still be described. A narrow interval is not a sufficient argument that all important errors have been addressed.

terms.definition: Agreement among repeated measurements.
A systematic tendency to overestimate or underestimate.
Real differences across the system rather than missing knowledge alone.

title: What Monte Carlo actually propagates
subtitle: Assess the assumptions behind a simulated interval.

sourceEvidence.needle: Monte Carlo simulation requires the analyst

paragraphs: Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis repeatedly evaluates a model using inputs drawn from specified probability distributions. The resulting collection of outputs provides a numerical description of the uncertainty implied by those input models and the calculation. The analyst must decide what the distributions represent and justify their parameters.

The method can accommodate complex calculations, asymmetric distributions and dependencies among inputs. However, those dependencies must be represented in the sampling procedure. Sampling every input independently is itself an assumption, not a feature that makes the analysis automatically correct.

More iterations generally improve the numerical precision of the simulation under the chosen setup. They do not repair a biased central estimate, an unjustified input distribution or missing processes. Reporting should therefore describe both the simulation procedure and the evidence supporting its uncertain inputs.

terms.definition: A description of the range and relative likelihood of possible values.
One repeated sampling and calculation cycle.
A relationship that affects how uncertain inputs vary together.

takeaway: A simulation propagates its assumptions as well as its input uncertainty.

title: When uncertain inputs move together
subtitle: Independence is an assumption that needs evidence.
paragraphs: Two uncertain inventory inputs may share measurements, estimation procedures or parameters. Their errors may therefore be dependent, even if the inputs appear in different categories or years. Treating them as independent can misrepresent uncertainty in a total or trend.

Dependence should be examined using knowledge of the data and methods. When suitable information is available, covariance or correlation can help describe it. A Monte Carlo analysis must then generate input combinations that respect the assumed relationships rather than sampling every quantity separately.

The effect of dependence is specific to the calculation and the relationships involved. It should not be assumed always negligible or always to increase uncertainty by a fixed amount. A transparent assessment identifies potentially important shared inputs and tests plausible alternative assumptions.

terms.definition: A statistical relationship in how quantities vary together.
A measure of joint departures from two means.
An assumption that knowing one uncertain input does not change the probability model for another.

title: Before transferring a factor to a new region
subtitle: Match the evidence to the population of interest.

sourceEvidence.needle: level of detail and coverage of the data match

paragraphs: Inventory data are useful only to the extent that their definitions and coverage match the estimate being constructed. Relevant dimensions include the sector, process, technology, location, substance and year. A large dataset from the wrong conditions may be less informative than a smaller dataset closely matched to the intended application.

When direct activity information is unavailable, an alternative or surrogate variable may be considered. Its use needs a defensible relationship to the target quantity, supporting statistical evidence and documentation of how the relationship is applied. A convenient correlation does not establish that a relationship transfers unchanged to every country.

An inventory compiler should also examine revisions, gaps and changes in data collection over time. The purpose is to build a coherent estimate rather than combine whatever numbers are easiest to obtain. Clear documentation makes the choices and remaining limitations visible to later users.

terms.definition: Correspondence between available data and the conditions of interest.
Alternative information used to approximate an unavailable target quantity.
An ordered sequence of observations or estimates over time.

title: An emission factor needs a compatible activity
subtitle: Use units and tiers to interpret an inventory calculation.

sourceEvidence.needle: Applying a Tier 1 emission estimate requires

paragraphs: For stationary-combustion greenhouse-gas estimates, the IPCC framework combines fuel consumed with an appropriate emission factor. When consumption is measured in energy units, the factor must be expressed on a compatible energy basis. A numerical product is meaningful only after the gas, fuel, units and category have been specified.

In a Tier 1 calculation, a default factor is combined with the activity data. A Tier 2 approach uses a country-specific factor intended to better represent national conditions. A more specific factor still needs supporting evidence, compatible units and transparent documentation; its label alone is not proof of quality.

Consider an illustrative calculation using 40 TJ of fuel and a factor of 50 kg of a specified gas per TJ. Their product is 2,000 kg of that gas. This example demonstrates unit cancellation, not a measured emission rate or a recommended factor. The chapter’s greenhouse-gas methods should not be assumed to cover every air pollutant.

terms.definition: Information about the scale of an emissions-related activity.
A coefficient connecting an activity to estimated releases.
Fuel burning in stationary equipment or installations.

questions.prompt: What does the illustrative product represent?

choices.text: 2,000 kg of the specified gas.
choices.explanation: TJ cancels, leaving kg of that gas.

choices.text: 2,000 TJ of fuel.
choices.explanation: Multiplying by kg per TJ leaves mass, not energy.

choices.text: 2,000 kg of every nitrogen species.
choices.explanation: The example is specific to one defined gas.

choices.text: A recommended universal emission factor.
choices.explanation: The passage explicitly labels the numbers illustrative.

questions.explanation: 40 TJ × 50 kg/TJ = 2,000 kg; the gas identity and scope remain essential.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the described Tier 2 approach from Tier 1?

choices.text: It removes the need for fuel consumption data.
choices.explanation: The activity data are still needed.

choices.text: It covers all air pollutants automatically.
choices.explanation: The stated scope is greenhouse-gas estimation.

choices.text: It makes unit conversion optional.
choices.explanation: Compatible units remain necessary.

choices.text: It uses a country-specific factor in place of a default factor.
choices.explanation: This is the distinction made in the passage.

questions.explanation: The factor becomes more specific, while the need for compatible activity data remains.

questions.prompt: Explain two checks needed before multiplying an activity dataset by an emission factor.
questions.modelAnswer: I would check that the units and energy or mass basis are compatible, and that the gas, fuel, category and period match. I would also assess whether the default or country-specific factor represents the intended conditions and whether an adjustment is already included.
rubric: Check unit compatibility and the basis of the factor.
Check substance and inventory boundaries.
Assess factor representativeness or document its limitations.
questions.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the reference points. Equivalent explanations are valid; this is self-assessment, not automated grading.

takeaway: Always keep units, substance identity and methodological scope attached to an inventory calculation.
